name: Nikhil Santos

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Nikhil. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to any AI company, employer, union, party or government, and we're not selling anything. Everything you tell me stays confidential, so you can say what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a dozer operator at a large open-pit coal mine. Most shifts I'm pushing overburden, that's the dirt and rock above the coal seam, or cleaning up around the shovels and building ramps. For the dangerous jobs near the high wall, I now run a remote-controlled dozer from a seat inside a converted shipping container at the edge of the pit, with screens and two joysticks. I like it, honestly, it's like a game where the stakes are real. What wears me out is the twelve-hour nights, at my age you feel them for two days.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: You like the remote seat. How did you end up doing that?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I asked. When they brought it in two years ago most of the older operators said no thanks, and I said yes please. I use AI every day, for managing our three rental units, for reading the machine fault codes, for planning my garden. Priya, my wife, runs the volunteer kitchen at our temple, our son Arjun's an engineer at the same coal company and our daughter Kavya's a dentist. I believe in hard work and family, and I think if you can see change coming, you should get in front of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: I'm going to read you five pictures of the future, one at a time. The first is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, the tools are useful, and the hype was just salesmen being salesmen. I'd post something sensible on the operators' group about how to use what we've got. No sense crying about the future that didn't come.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think AI Plateau means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means I keep pushing dirt until sixty-three or so, keep the rentals, and retire comfortably. The coal itself has a time limit anyway, the mine's got maybe fifteen years left. So I've always planned for an ending.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep working the remote seat when they need me. Keep using the assistant for the rentals and the paperwork. I'd look at buying a fourth unit if the prices are right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A little flat, I like a bit of movement.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You use AI daily. What does AI Plateau mean for your rental units and side plans?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It does the tenant letters, reminds me about maintenance, checks the leases. I used to spend Sunday afternoons on that, now it's twenty minutes. That's enough for me in this picture.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything you'd do with your savings in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe the fourth unit. I'd rather own bricks than a pension fund I can't see. Priya says three's plenty, we'd argue about it nicely.

S0.say: I'd say the tools are useful and the hype was just salesmen being salesmen, and I'd post on the operators' group about using what we've got. No sense crying about a future that didn't come.
S0.think: He expects to keep pushing dirt until about sixty-three, keep the rentals and retire comfortably. The coal mine has maybe fifteen years left anyway, so he has always planned for an ending.
S0.do: Keeps working the remote dozer seat when needed and uses the AI assistant for the rentals and paperwork. Considers buying a fourth rental unit if prices are right.
S0.feel: Calm and a little flat, since he likes a bit of movement.
S0.quote: I'd rather own bricks than a pension fund I can't see.
S0.fieldNote: Nikhil is already running a remote dozer and asked for the job when others refused. His security is spread across savings and three rental units. He knows his coal mine has its own end date, so endings don't scare him.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say get in front of it, don't wait for the government or the union to save you. Learn the new machines, ask for the training. I'd tell the young ones in the crib room that the man who asks first gets the good seat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think Steady Disruption means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I think it's good for me. I'm already in the remote seat, so I'm the kind of operator they'll keep. I'd worry more about the guys who said no thanks two years ago.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask to train on the full autonomous dozer system and become one of the people who supervise a fleet. On my days off I'd look at buying a used dozer, fitting it with an autonomy kit and doing farm dams and land clearing as a small contracting business. I've already priced it, about the cost of a small apartment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, a bit excited. This is the picture I'd pick if I could.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you blame, if anyone, for jobs shrinking?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nobody, really. Businesses do what makes sense and the market decides. If a man won't learn, I'm sorry for him, but that's partly on him.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the coal running out. Does that change your plans here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It makes me hurry. If the coal runs out in fifteen years and the machines take more tasks anyway, I want my own little business going before I retire, so I'm not relying on one company.

S1.say: I'd say get in front of it and don't wait for the government or union to save you; learn the new machines and ask for training. The one who asks first gets the good seat.
S1.think: He thinks it's good for him, since he's already in the remote seat and is the kind of operator they'll keep. His worry is for those who turned down the remote work two years ago.
S1.do: Trains on the full autonomous dozer system to supervise a fleet. Prices a used dozer fitted with an autonomy kit to start a small farm dam and land-clearing contracting business on his days off.
S1.feel: Calm and a bit excited, the picture he'd choose if he could.
S1.quote: I'd tell the young ones in the crib room that the man who asks first gets the good seat.
S1.fieldNote: His free-market views show in blaming no one and expecting people to learn. He would actually bring automation into his own small contracting business. Coal's limited life adds urgency to his plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's too fast, and people need to look after their families and stick together. I'd say the community, the temple, the families should carry each other through. I wouldn't say the government should take over, that never ends well.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think AGI by 2028 means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think even the supervisor job goes, the AI can watch a fleet better than me. My contracting plan probably goes too, because a farmer will buy his own robot dozer. I'd be fine with the rentals and savings, but my clever plans would be worth less than I thought.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First week, I'd talk to Priya and the kids and look at the numbers. I'd take a package at sixty if they offered one, and I'd shift some savings into companies that make the machines. I'd keep the rental units, because people still need roofs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Like getting to the station early and the train's already left.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With full AGI in two years, does even the fleet supervisor job last?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably not for long. Maybe a year or two of setting things up, then the AI watches the AI. I'd still go for it, because a year of good pay is a year of good pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Arjun, who works for the same company?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell him to think about what humans will still want from humans. Engineering might be safe longer, or might not. I'd tell him we'd help with money if he needs to retrain, that's what family does.

S2.say: I'd say it's too fast and people should look after their families and stick together, with community, temple and families carrying each other. I wouldn't say the government should take over.
S2.think: He believes even the fleet supervisor job goes and his contracting plan too, since farmers would buy their own robot dozers. He'd be fine on rentals and savings, but his clever plans would be worth less than he thought.
S2.do: Talks through the numbers with his wife and children in the first week and takes a package at sixty if offered. Shifts some savings into machine-making companies and keeps the rental units.
S2.feel: Uneasy, like arriving early at the station only to find the train already gone.
S2.quote: Like getting to the station early and the train's already left.
S2.fieldNote: Two years defeats his strategy of getting in front of change. His fallback is property and family rather than the state. He offers to fund his son's retraining, showing his family-first values.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is plenty for anyone who's willing to work. Learn, save, plan. And look after your own.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think AGI by 2031 means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is enough for me to get the remote and fleet jobs, earn well, and build the contracting business a bit before it's swallowed. I'd retire around sixty-three with more than I'd planned. Honestly it's a good picture for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Year one, train on the autonomous fleet system and move into supervising. Buy the used dozer and the autonomy kit, start the contracting on weekends. Put a bit of savings into the machine makers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Busy and calm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How is five years different for you, compared with two?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, in this one. Five years is enough to make back the money and some more, before every farmer has his own robot. Then I'd sell the dozer and the client list to someone younger.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you go ahead with the contracting business in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years, the train's gone. Five years, I'm on it and I've got a good seat. That's the whole difference.

S3.say: I'd say five years is plenty for anyone willing to work: learn, save, plan and look after your own.
S3.think: He thinks five years is enough to get the remote and fleet jobs, earn well and build his contracting business before it's swallowed. He'd retire around sixty-three with more than planned, so it's a good picture for him.
S3.do: Trains on the autonomous fleet system and moves into supervising in year one. Buys a used dozer with an autonomy kit to start weekend contracting, and invests some savings in machine makers.
S3.quote: Then I'd sell the dozer and the client list to someone younger.
S3.fieldNote: Five years is enough for his adaptability and appetite for risk to pay off. He plans an exit from his own business, treating it like an investment. His train metaphor carries through from the fast picture.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years, no excuses. Anyone who isn't ready by then didn't try. I'd say it kindly, but I'd say it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think AGI by 2036 means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be retired with the rentals and maybe the contracting business sold. It doesn't threaten me. If anything it's interesting to watch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep working, train on the new systems as they come, build the contracting business over a few years. Retire around sixty-three. Keep the rentals and maybe buy one more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Comfortable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: By 2036 you'd be sixty-eight. What does this one look like for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want them to have a strong family, a faith, and a skill people still pay for. The machines will do the work, but someone has to decide what's worth doing. I'd want them to be the deciders.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want for your grandchildren?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Priya says I should slow down by then. Maybe I will. Maybe I'll just fly drones over the garden, she can't stop me.

S4.say: I'd say ten years means no excuses, and anyone who isn't ready by then didn't try. I'd say it kindly, but I'd say it.
S4.think: He expects to be retired with the rentals and perhaps the contracting business sold, so it doesn't threaten him. If anything it's interesting to watch.
S4.do: Keeps working and trains on new systems as they arrive, building the contracting business over a few years. Retires around sixty-three, keeps the rentals and may buy one more.
S4.quote: The machines will do the work, but someone has to decide what's worth doing.
S4.fieldNote: With ten years he sees AGI as interesting to watch from a comfortable retirement. He is firm but not harsh about personal responsibility. His hopes for his grandchildren mix faith, family and judgment.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because it beats even the people who try to get ahead, and it would hit Arjun's generation hard. What would help is time, honestly, and a community that sticks together, with families and the temple helping each other more than waiting on the government.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about coal. Our mine has a closing date AGI or not, so some of us have been planning for the end for years. Maybe that's why I'm not as scared as you'd expect.

headlineQuote: It's like a game where the stakes are real.
portrait: Nikhil Santos is a 58-year-old dozer operator at a large open-pit coal mine who volunteered for the remote-controlled dozer when older colleagues refused. He uses AI daily, owns three rental units and believes in hard work, family and getting in front of change. In the slower pictures he plans to supervise an autonomous fleet and start his own small contracting business with a robot dozer. The two-year AGI picture leaves him financially secure but uneasy that even early movers get beaten. With five or ten years he is calm and comfortable, leaning on property, family and his temple community.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries him most, because it beats even people who try to get ahead and would hit his son's generation hard.
whatWouldHelp: Time, and a community that sticks together, with families and the temple helping each other rather than waiting on government.
